CHAPTER 12

Learning to Learn
学会学习

Live as if you were to die tomorrow. Learn as if you were to live forever.
——Mahatma Gandhi

活着，如同明日将死；学习，如同永生不死。
——圣雄甘地

If you’ve been in the technology space for any length of time, you’re familiar with the reality that technology changes. Constantly. Which means you will be challenged to learn new things regularly. Many engineers believe they are paid to write code, which is true. However, you are also paid to think. You earn a living by using your brain, so you have to feed your brains with knowledge, which means learning.

只要在技术圈子里待过一段时间，你就熟悉这样一个现实：技术在变。而且一直在变。这意味着你将不断面临学习新事物的挑战。很多工程师认为自己是被雇来写代码的，这没错。然而，你也是被雇来思考的。你靠大脑谋生，所以必须用知识喂养大脑，这就意味着学习。

Arguably, the ability to learn new things quickly is the most important skill of a successful engineer. Additionally, you need to not only understand new things but also apply what you’ve learned to real-world scenarios. Many people benefit from the “see one, do one, teach one” approach.

可以说，快速学习新事物的能力是成功工程师最重要的技能。此外，你不仅要理解新事物，还要把学到的东西应用到真实场景中。很多人从“看一次、做一次、教一次”的方法中受益。

The Shiny New Thing Paradox
闪亮新事物悖论

Software engineers are attracted to “new” like moths to a flame, and when something first appears, it is often accompanied by a flurry of activity that makes it seem like you’ll be left behind if you don’t immediately embrace it. In the early days though, technologies might not be ready for prime time; the rough edges haven’t been sanded down yet. Over time, the hype fades. But that is often when the new thing is most ready for adoption. Never forget, new technologies are like buses: another one will come along in 15 minutes.
软件工程师被“新”吸引，就像飞蛾扑火。当某个东西刚出现时，往往伴随着一阵热闹，让你觉得不立刻拥抱它就会被淘汰。但在早期，技术可能还没准备好登上大舞台；粗糙的边角还没打磨。随着时间推移，炒作褪去。而那往往正是新事物最适合被采用的时候。永远记住，新技术就像公交车：15 分钟后又会来一辆。

Cramming Doesn’t Work

Odds are at some point in your educational career you crammed for an important test. And it might have succeeded—at least in the short term. But did you retain the information? To truly learn something, you must encode the information: it must be elaborate, meaningful, and have context. Stories are incredibly effective and have been used for millennia to teach and share. Learning often involves repetition and, when spaced out appropriately, increases knowledge and retention.

在你求学的某个阶段，你很可能为一场重要考试临时抱过佛脚。而且它可能奏效了——至少短期内如此。但你记住那些信息了吗？要真正学会某样东西，你必须把信息编码：它必须是详尽的、有意义的、有上下文的。故事极其有效，几千年来一直被用来教学和分享。学习往往需要重复，而当重复被适当地间隔开时，能增长知识、提升记忆保持率。

How do stories apply to you as an engineer? It’s one thing to have someone tell you to be very careful when using commands like rm, especially with the -f flag. It is something altogether different for someone to share the story about how they inadvertently wiped their laptop hard drive while working on a script that included rm -f.1

作为工程师，故事怎么用在你身上？有人告诉你用 rm 这类命令要非常小心，尤其是带 -f 参数时，这是一回事；而有人跟你分享他写脚本时不小心用 rm -f 把笔记本硬盘清空的故事，那完全是另一回事。1

Despite your best efforts, you will forget things, which is actually a feature, not a bug! Your brain is incredibly good at purging information you no longer need. While some bits may never leave,2 and others vanish far too quickly,3 your brain is actively “taking out the trash,” as it were. Information decay is predictable, but it isn’t the same for everyone or every fact. Computers can help by repeating questions at proven intervals (which, along with some pretty slick gamification, is how some people succeed at learning new languages). Some of you have likely availed yourself of the low-tech but very effective technique of leveraging flash cards!

不管你多努力，你都会忘事——这其实是个特性，而不是 bug！你的大脑非常擅长清理你不再需要的信息。虽然有些信息永远不会离开，2 另一些消失得太快，3 但你的大脑可以说是在积极地“倒垃圾”。信息遗忘是可预测的，但对每个人、每条事实都不一样。计算机可以帮上忙：按经过验证的间隔重复提问（再加上一些相当精巧的游戏化机制，这就是有些人成功学会新语言的方式）。你们中有些人很可能已经用过那种低技术但非常有效的闪卡技巧！

If you find yourself struggling with something, it is often better to put it aside for a bit rather than continuing to beat your head against the wall. The simple act of taking a shower, going for a walk, or making dinner can distract you enough to unleash the answer. Your brain has two distinct processing modes: R-mode and L-mode. R-mode is the nonverbal, search-and-retrieve aspect of your brain. It runs in the background and isn’t directly controllable, which leads to some unpredictable results. When you’re watching a movie and you can’t quite remember that actor’s name—and then five minutes later it just pops into your head—that’s the R-mode at work. The L-mode, by contrast, is verbal, analytical, and linear and is focused on logic and computation. By distracting the L-mode, you can free up the R-mode to do what it does best. Think about the problem and then do something routine like taking a shower or cleaning up the house.

如果你发现自己在某件事上卡住了，往往最好先把它放一放，而不是继续拿头撞墙。简简单单洗个澡、散个步、做个饭，就能足够分散你的注意力，让答案冒出来。你的大脑有两种不同的处理模式：R 模式和 L 模式。R 模式是大脑中非语言、负责搜索和提取的那一面。它在后台运行，无法直接控制，因此会产生一些不可预测的结果。当你看电影时想不起那个演员的名字——然后五分钟后它突然跳进你脑子里——那就是 R 模式在起作用。相比之下，L 模式是语言的、分析的、线性的，专注于逻辑和计算。通过分散 L 模式的注意力，你可以释放 R 模式去做它最擅长的事。先想想问题，然后去做些常规的事，比如洗个澡或收拾房子。

1 Someone your authors may or may not have direct experience with themselves.
你们的作者自己可能——也可能没有——亲身经历过。
2 Say, a phone number from your youth or the name of your favorite elementary school teacher.
比如你年轻时记的一个电话号码，或者你最喜欢的小学老师的名字。
3 What did you say your name was again?
你刚才说你叫什么名字来着？
原书第 294 页

As an engineer, you can use these two processing modes to your advantage. If you find yourself stuck on an issue, pushing harder might not be the most effective solution. Don’t be afraid to put the issue aside for a bit, distract the L-mode by doing a more mundane task (or take a walk), and see what happens. More often than not, a solution will spring to mind later.

作为工程师，你可以利用这两种处理模式为自己服务。如果你发现自己被某个问题卡住，更用力地推未必是最有效的解法。不要害怕把问题放一放，做点更平凡的事分散 L 模式的注意力（或者去散个步），看看会发生什么。通常，一个解决方案稍后会自己冒出来。

Skills Acquisition

The best investment you can make is in yourself. The more you learn, the more you earn.
——Warren Buffett, American investor and philanthropist

你能做的最好的投资，就是投资你自己。你学得越多，赚得越多。
——Warren Buffett，美国投资人、慈善家

There are several models of skills acquisition that all have similar concepts. One example that comes out of the martial arts is Shu Ha Ri, or as Bruce Lee once said, “Learn the principle, abide by the principle, and dissolve the principle.” Another way of thinking about this comes from Clark Terry: Imitate, Assimilate, Innovate.

技能习得有好几种模型，它们的概念都相似。一个来自武术的例子是“守破离”，或者用 Bruce Lee 的话说：“学习原则、恪守原则、然后消解原则。”另一种说法来自 Clark Terry：模仿、吸收、创新。

In the Shu or Imitate phase, students follow the instructor exactly. The focus is on duplicating the teacher without much concern for the why or the underlying theory. In the Ha stage, you start to branch out. You understand the basics and have enough muscle memory to repeat the core movements. Now is when you begin to fill in the theory and start to seek out other teachers or sources of information, which you can then assimilate into your understanding of the topic. At the Ri stage, you are learning from yourself, essentially. Your practice drives the learning instead of following the path laid out by others.

在“守”或模仿阶段，学生完全跟随导师。重点是复制老师，不太关心为什么或背后的理论。在“破”阶段，你开始分支。你理解了基础，有足够的肌肉记忆来重复核心动作。这时你开始填补理论，并主动寻找其他老师或信息来源，然后把它们吸收进你对这个主题的理解。在“离”阶段，你基本上是在向自己学习。是你的实践在驱动学习，而不是跟随别人铺好的路。

The Dreyfus model expands on this concept by dividing learning into five distinct stages (outlined in Figure 12-1) that work in a progression. In the Novice stage, learners require recipes: do this exact thing. If you’re learning a new sport, this is the stage when your coach might move your foot a few degrees or have you repeat a move seemingly endlessly. At the Advanced Beginner stage, you start to move beyond the rigid rules; you start experimenting to see what happens when you change your grip or modify a stance.

Dreyfus 模型扩展了这个概念，把学习分成五个不同的阶段（见图 12-1），按顺序推进。在新手阶段，学习者需要菜谱式的指导：做这件确切的事。如果你在学一项新运动，这就是教练把你的脚挪几度、或者让你没完没了重复一个动作的阶段。在高级初学者阶段，你开始跳出死板规则；你开始实验，看看改变握法或调整站姿会发生什么。

At the Competent stage, you can start to troubleshoot. You may recognize what your mistake was by watching the ball flight. If you make it to the Proficient stage, you can self-correct. You can see or feel the mistake and fix it without needing a coach to point it out. If you work at something long enough, you’ll enter the Expert stage, where it all happens by intuition. As a golfer, you just think, “I need this ball to cut” and…it cuts! In fact, at this stage, you’d likely struggle to explain what or how you accomplished something; it just seemed right.

在胜任阶段，你可以开始排查问题。你也许能通过观察球的飞行轨迹认出自己错在哪里。如果你到达精通阶段，你可以自我纠正。你能看到或感觉到错误，不需要教练指出来就能修正。如果你在某件事上钻研得足够久，就会进入专家阶段，一切都凭直觉发生。作为高尔夫球手，你只是想：“我需要这球切出去”——然后它就切了！事实上，在这个阶段，你很可能很难解释自己做了什么、怎么做的；它就是感觉对。

原书第 295 页

It should be clear that telling someone who just picked up a golf club to “hit a cut by thinking about hitting a cut” won’t work very well. When you are just starting out, you need step-by-step instructions, which is why so many languages and frameworks have Getting Started tutorials.4 Rules and recipes are vital to beginners, but they can absolutely stifle experts because they inhibit their hard-earned intuition. And just as with improving your short game, simply watching a video or reading tip will take you only so far: you have to practice!

显然，告诉一个刚拿起高尔夫球杆的人“想着切球就能切出去”不会有什么效果。刚开始时，你需要循序渐进的指导，这就是为什么这么多语言和框架都有入门教程。4 规则和菜谱对初学者至关重要，但它们也会扼杀专家——因为它们压制了专家辛苦得来的直觉。就像提升你的短杆技术一样，光看视频或读技巧只能带你走这么远：你必须练习！

Think about how you learn a new framework. Do you immediately jump into building a complex application? Probably not. You start with the proverbial “Hello World!” example.5 At first, you’re copying code directly out of a tutorial, relying on search or a chatbot to troubleshoot errors. Over time though, your intuition develops, and you start to recognize patterns; you’ll know where the problem is as soon as you see the error message. After even more time, you’ll discover where the edges of the map are, the parts of the framework that you’d change if you could. As you approach mastery, you’ll no longer be translating what you want; you’ll simply be expressing your intent through the framework. When given a task, you’ll “see” how to do it.

想想你是怎么学一个新框架的。你会立刻跳进去构建一个复杂应用吗？大概不会。你从大家都知道的“Hello World!”例子开始。5 一开始，你直接从教程里复制代码，靠搜索或聊天机器人排查错误。但随着时间推移，你的直觉发展起来，开始识别模式；一看到错误信息，你就知道问题在哪。再过一段时间，你会发现地图的边缘在哪里——框架里那些你如果能改就会改的部分。当你接近精通时，你不再翻译自己想要什么；你只是通过框架表达意图。接到任务时，你会“看到”该怎么做。

4 Plus, who doesn’t need another to-do list, amirite?
再说，谁不需要又一个待办清单呢，对吧？
5 How many to-do list applications have you built?
你自己写过多少个待办清单应用了？

The Learning Habit

The most important skill to have as a programmer is the ability to teach yourself new things effectively and efficiently. You’re going to be constantly growing and picking up new technologies. The ability to do that is more important than any individual tool or technology.
——Ali Spittel, software engineer

作为程序员，最重要的技能是高效、有效地自学新事物的能力。你会不断成长、不断接触新技术。这种能力比任何具体工具或技术都重要。
——Ali Spittel，软件工程师

While there are few hard-and-fast rules, becoming an expert takes a significant amount of time, which is why most people don’t go much beyond advanced beginner. Given the pace technology moves, that has startling ramifications. Technology moves fast; how much time do you get with something before you move on to the next big thing? That isn’t to say a successful career requires you to become an expert on every aspect of software. Over your career, your expertise will grow in some areas while other skills remain in the advanced beginner phase, and there’s nothing wrong with that!

虽然没有什么铁律，但成为专家需要大量时间，这就是为什么大多数人不会走得太远，停在高级初学者阶段。考虑到技术演进的速度，这带来了惊人的后果。技术跑得快；在你转向下一个大事件之前，你有多少时间泡在某样东西上？这并不是说成功的职业生涯要求你成为软件每个方面的专家。在你的职业生涯中，你的专长会在某些领域成长，而另一些技能停留在高级初学者阶段——这完全没问题！

The challenge is getting the most out of your limited learning time. Make a list of what you want to explore, prioritizing what you want to learn over the next few months. Your list and priorities will be fluid; as your interests change, so too will your learning goals.

挑战在于把你有限的学习时间用到极致。列一张你想探索的清单，按未来几个月想学什么排优先级。你的清单和优先级会变化；随着兴趣改变，学习目标也会改变。

Not all learning requires the same level of focus or attention: the depth you choose to pursue changes based on the topic. Christopher Judd refers to this approach as a Learning Depth Strategy:

不是所有学习都需要同样程度的专注或注意力：你选择钻研的深度随主题而变。Christopher Judd 把这种方法称为“学习深度策略”：

  • Survey: Listen to podcasts, attend user group or conference sessions, watch technology conference keynotes, peruse the release notes.概览：听播客，参加用户组或会议分场，看技术会议主题演讲，翻翻发布说明。
  • Shallow dive: Watch short videos, read blog posts and articles, work through tutorials.浅潜：看短视频，读博客和文章，跟着教程做。
  • Deep dive: Attend a live, in-person or online workshop or training course, read books about the topic.深潜：参加线下或线上的实战工作坊或培训课程，读相关书籍。
  • Ultra deep dive: Deliver a presentation on the topic or lead a workshop or training class.超深潜：就这个主题做一次演讲，或主持一个工作坊或培训班。

Learning has to be a habit as humans forget things. In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus studied memory, discovering people forgot half of what they learned a mere 30 minutes after learning it! However, when you are repeatedly exposed to the material, the decay slows considerably. He proposed the idea of spaced repetition: essentially, reviewing the material at gradually increasing intervals after you learn it reinforces the concepts before they are completely lost. Consider how you could schedule this approach throughout your year:

学习必须成为习惯，因为人会忘事。1880 年代，Hermann Ebbinghaus 研究记忆，发现人们在学完 30 分钟后就忘掉一半！然而，当你反复接触材料时，遗忘会大幅减慢。他提出了间隔重复的概念：本质上，在你学完之后按逐渐增大的间隔复习材料，能在概念完全丢失之前强化它。想想你可以如何在一整年里安排这种方法：

原书第 297 页
  • Weekly: Listen to podcasts, watch a video or two, read an article or two.每周：听播客，看一两个视频，读一两篇文章。
  • Monthly: Read a technical or business book, attend a user group or meetup, take an online course.每月：读一本技术或商业书，参加一次用户组或聚会，上一门在线课程。
  • Yearly: Attend a technical conference, learn a new programming language, invest in a side project, get a certification, teach or deliver a technical presentation.每年：参加一次技术会议，学一门新编程语言，投入一个副业项目，考一个认证，教一次课或做一次技术演讲。

It can also be helpful to “learn out loud.” Consider posting your progress on social media; you will often discover a community of like-minded people offering support and encouragement. As you uncover new things, think about creating a video or write-up of what you’ve learned; don’t be surprised when a future search on a question returns something you’ve created!6 You’ll be thankful you took the time to document what you did.

“大声学习”也会有帮助。考虑把你的进展发到社交媒体上；你常常会发现一群志同道合的人提供支持和鼓励。当你发现新东西时，考虑做一个视频或写一篇文章记录你学到的东西；以后搜索某个问题时，如果返回的是你自己写的东西，别惊讶！6 你会感谢自己花时间记录了所做的事。

The Technology Merry-Go-Round
技术旋转木马

Nate here. Early in my career, I was talking to my then manager and asked why they’d moved out of tech into management. They told me they were tired of having to constantly learn new things, of always being on the technology merry-go-round; they’d seen enough new things! While I didn’t fully appreciate that insight newly out of university, I completely understand the sentiment today. How many languages or frameworks or frontend libraries or datastores have you learned in your career? That isn’t to say management is the path of least resistance: there are plenty of unique challenges guiding people. But being a software engineer means a near constant stream of adding to your knowledge portfolio. It can be very invigorating, but don’t underestimate how hard it can be either.
Nate 来说两句。职业生涯早期，我和当时的经理聊天，问他为什么从技术岗转去做管理。他告诉我，他厌倦了不断学新东西，厌倦了永远待在技术旋转木马上；他已经看够了新东西！刚出校门时我并不完全理解这句话，但今天我完全理解这种感受。你职业生涯里学过多少种语言、框架、前端库、数据存储？这并不是说管理是阻力最小的路：带人有一大堆独特的挑战。但做软件工程师意味着几乎要不停地往自己的知识组合里加东西。这让人非常振奋，但也不要低估它有多难。
6 Both of your authors can attest to finding some of their own material they had completely forgotten they’d created.
你们的两位作者都可以作证，他们都找到过自己完全忘了写过的东西。

Knowing there will always be more to learn, how do you keep up? You need to make it a habit. Develop a routine that works for you. Block out time on your calendar to read and explore; you may have to schedule over it from time to time. Friday afternoons are generally quieter,7 but maybe for you it is Tuesday morning or Thursday over lunch. Ultimately, you must be the guardian of your own time. Some people plot out a year’s worth of learning on a Trello board or set reminders throughout the calendar. Experiment with what works best for you, but whatever you do, set aside specific blocks of time to learn.

既然知道永远有更多东西要学，你怎么跟得上？你需要把它变成习惯。养成一套适合自己的惯例。在日历上留出时间阅读和探索；你可能不得不时不时地把它往后推。周五下午通常比较安静，7 但对你来说也许是周二早上或周四午饭时间。最终，你必须做自己时间的守护者。有些人在 Trello 看板上规划一整年的学习，或在日历上设置提醒。试试哪种最适合你，但无论如何，都要留出专门的时间块来学习。

You should strongly consider a practice we refer to as morning coffee. Take the first 15–30 minutes of your day, when you’re sitting down with your preferred beverage (whether it’s a shot of espresso, tea, an energy drink, or something else) and peruse the news, whatever that means for you. It could be spending some time on social media, listening to a podcast, walking through a tutorial, or reading an early edition of a new tech book. But make it a habit and do it before your day gets away from you. You’ve had those days that just seem to disappear down a rabbit hole of fire drills! Prioritizing that time will also help on those days where you were so busy you felt like you didn’t get anything done; at least you’ve learned something new!

你应该认真考虑一种我们称为“晨间咖啡”的做法。拿出一天的头 15–30 分钟，当你坐下来享用自己喜欢的饮料时（不管是一杯意式浓缩、茶、能量饮料还是别的什么），浏览一下新闻——对你来说那是什么都行。可能是在社交媒体上泡一会儿，听一档播客，过一遍教程，或者读一本新技术书的初稿。但把它变成习惯，在你的一天失控之前做掉它。你一定有过那种日子：一天就这么消失在救火的兔子洞里！把这段时间排在优先位置，也会在那种你忙到觉得自己什么都没干的日子里帮到你；至少你学到了新东西！

Learning Through AI

AI can be a learning accelerator. While it isn’t a substitute for hands-on experience, using a chatbot can help you research topics. Chatbots can be great resources for tailored learning paths and deep-diving technology in a conversational, digestible manner. For example, let’s say you need to use a Java class you aren’t familiar with or want more info on a reference model. You certainly can read the docs, but you can also have AI do it for you, as seen in Figures 12-2 and 12-3.

AI 可以是学习加速器。虽然它不能替代动手经验，但用聊天机器人可以帮你调研主题。聊天机器人可以很好地提供定制化学习路径，并以对话式、易于消化的方式深入技术。例如，假设你需要用一个你不熟悉的 Java 类，或想了解一个参考模型。你当然可以读文档，但也可以让 AI 替你读，如图 12-2 和图 12-3 所示。

7 Anyone who schedules a meeting on a Friday afternoon has committed a hostile act.
任何在周五下午安排会议的人，都犯下了敌对行为。

原书第 300 页

You do need to be aware of hallucinations, and you should double-check with the source material, but there’s no doubt AI can help you learn new information and brush up on concepts from your past.

你确实需要警惕幻觉，并对照原始材料再三核实，但毫无疑问，AI 可以帮你学习新知识、重温过去学过的概念。

Fear of Missing Out

There are a lot of bits out there: new languages, new techniques, new approaches. How do you keep up? Your preferred learning style has a lot to say about your approach. Some people prefer to read articles and books, some prefer to listen or watch, while others learn best by doing. There is no shortage of learning sources at your disposal, from searching the web, following a reading list, listening to podcasts, watching videos, attending user groups and conferences, and leveraging industry resources like the Technology Radar.

外面有海量信息：新语言、新技术、新方法。你怎么跟得上？你偏好的学习方式很大程度上决定了你的做法。有些人喜欢读文章和书，有些人喜欢听或看，还有些人动手学得最好。你可用的学习来源不胜枚举：搜索网络、按阅读清单读、听播客、看视频、参加用户组和会议，以及利用像技术雷达这样的行业资源。

Attention is a precious resource, and you can’t just scale it up. Don’t waste it. You cannot read or watch or listen to everything; you are going to have to be selective. Many developers have a legitimate fear of missing out (FOMO), where if they aren’t actively consuming “everything,” something vital will slip by.

注意力是宝贵的资源，你没法简单地放大它。别浪费。你不可能读完、看完、听完一切；你必须有所选择。很多开发者真的有错失恐惧症（FOMO）：如果不主动消费“一切”，某个重要的东西就会溜走。

Sorry to burst your bubble, but you literally cannot read or watch or listen to everything. In fact, in the time it takes you to read this paragraph, roughly another week’s worth of video will have been uploaded to YouTube! And that doesn’t take into account podcasts or Getting Started guides or social media or any other content you might want to consume.

抱歉打破你的幻想，但你真的不可能读完、看完、听完一切。事实上，在你读这一段的时间里，YouTube 上大概又上传了相当于一周量的视频！这还没算播客、入门指南、社交媒体或任何你可能想消费的内容。

Technology FOMO is real, but take solace in the reality that if something really big happens in technology, you will hear about it. You might miss the initial announcement, but that’s OK. Heck, there are areas you aren’t overly interested in but you still heard about! Don’t be afraid to leverage your network too. Odds are your friends and colleagues all have different interests than you. Take advantage of that. In fact, you could share interesting information you find in your specialization areas with them, and vice versa. There’s nothing wrong with sharding your learning across multiple people!

技术 FOMO 是真实存在的，但请这样安慰自己：如果技术圈真出了大事，你一定会听说。你可能错过最初的宣布，但没关系。说实话，有些领域你根本不太感兴趣，但你还是听说了！也不要害怕利用你的人脉。你的朋友和同事很可能和你兴趣不同。利用这一点。事实上，你可以把你在自己专业领域发现的有趣信息分享给他们，反之亦然。把学习分片到多个人身上没什么不对！

Focus means you won’t get to surf every wave in the ocean.
——Kelsey Hightower, American software engineer, developer advocate

专注意味着你不会去追海里的每一道浪。
——Kelsey Hightower，美国软件工程师、开发者布道师

Your time and attention are incredibly valuable resources.8 And they are resources: you can’t just scale them up. You cannot afford to waste your attention; you must be selective with how you spend it. Don’t practice resume-driven development; you need a why to learn something new. There will always be another hot new thing on social media, and it’s OK to wait to learn something until you need it. Evaluating a new technology is tricky, but with experience you’ll start to spot the patterns, and you’ll see how this “new” thing is actually very similar to something from a few years back.

你的时间和注意力是极其宝贵的资源。8 而且它们是资源：你没法简单地放大它们。你浪费不起自己的注意力；你必须对怎么花它有所选择。不要做简历驱动开发；你需要一个“为什么”去学新东西。社交媒体上永远有下一个热门新事物，等到需要时再学也完全可以。评估新技术很棘手，但随着经验积累，你会开始识别模式，会发现这个“新”东西其实和几年前的某个东西非常像。

8 Time is a nonrenewable resource. Use it wisely.
时间是不可再生资源。明智地使用它。

If your instincts tell you something is overhyped, there’s nothing wrong with taking a beat before investing time in it.

如果你的直觉告诉你某样东西被过度炒作了，在投入时间之前先停一停，没什么不对。

Your professional network can be very useful here as well, as sometimes you can outsource the learning to someone else. If you know a friend is exploring a space you’re not sure of just yet, touch base with them periodically to see how it’s going. Their experience can guide you, and in some cases they’ll work through problems, allowing you to skip over some rough patches.

你的职业人脉在这里也很有用，因为有时候你可以把学习外包给别人。如果你知道一个朋友正在探索一个你还不确定的领域，定期和他联系，看看进展如何。他们的经验可以指导你，有些情况下他们会把问题趟过去，让你跳过一些坑坑洼洼。

注意力有点像房地产：不会再有更多了。但和房地产不同的是，它的价值还在不断上升。

Let Your Passion Guide You
让你的热情指引你

Nate here. I once tried to learn more about databases so I sat down on a random day and started going through a book on the topic. After about 20 minutes, I put the book down and literally went upstairs and organized my sock drawer. Not a euphemism: I decided my sock drawer was a higher priority. That was an unambiguous signal I did not, in fact, have a passion for the particular topic of databases. While you can schedule some learning time pretty easily, that still leaves a rather important question: what should you be studying? Ultimately, this is up to you, but you should let your passion guide you. If you aren’t excited about a topic, you’ll find it difficult to make time in your day to practice.
Nate 来说两句。有一次我想多学一点数据库，就在某个随便的日子坐下来开始看一本相关的书。大约 20 分钟后，我合上书，真的上楼去整理我的袜子抽屉了。这不是委婉说法：我判断我的袜子抽屉优先级更高。这是一个明确的信号：我其实对数据库这个主题没有热情。虽然你可以很容易地安排学习时间，但这仍然留下一个相当重要的问题：你应该学什么？最终，这取决于你自己，但你应该让热情指引你。如果你对一个主题不兴奋，就很难在一天中挤出时间去练。
Pick something that energizes you and go deep on it. Follow the experts, listen to the podcasts, watch the videos, and read the documentation. Read “Find What You’re Passionate About” on page 306. Keep in mind you can switch to something different at any time. There’s nothing wrong with putting a book down or closing a tab or leaving a video half watched; there aren’t extra points for finishing. If you’re still excited about a given topic, great, keep going! If it no longer sparks joy, fantastic, pick something new. Rinse and repeat.
选一件让你充满能量的事，深入下去。追随专家，听播客，看视频，读文档。参见第 306 页的“找到你的热情所在”。记住，你可以随时切换到别的东西。把书放下、关掉标签页、看到一半就离开视频，都没什么不对；看完并不会加分。如果你对某个主题仍然兴奋，很好，继续！如果它不再让你心动，太棒了，换个新东西。如此反复。

Just as you cannot keep up with every new thing in software, you also can’t adopt every new thing either. Your passion about a given tool or technology doesn’t automatically mean it is a good fit for your project or organization. Many developers have, at one time or another, practiced resume-driven development. In other words, they adopted a new technology because they wanted to add it to their resume, not because it would meaningfully benefit the project.

正如你跟不上软件里的每一件新事物一样，你也不能采用每一件新事物。你对某个工具或技术的热情，并不自动意味着它适合你的项目或组织。很多开发者都曾做过简历驱动开发。换句话说，他们采用一项新技术是因为想把它加到简历上，而不是因为它能切实地让项目受益。

You must be a critical consumer of new things. Software is a constant set of trade-offs, and despite the way it is often taught, there is rarely a “best” way.9 Don’t focus on just

你必须成为新事物的批判性消费者。软件是一连串不断的权衡；尽管教它的时候常被说成有最优解，但其实很少有“最好”的方式。9 不要只盯着

9 More often than not, you are choosing the least worst approach.
很多时候，你只是在选一个“最不差”的方案。

the positives of a technology, but consider all of the consequences. Be an informed consumer and remember Rich Hickey’s wise words: “Programmers know the benefits of everything and the trade-offs of nothing.”

一项技术的正面，而要考虑所有后果。做一个知情的消费者，记住 Rich Hickey 的智慧之言：“程序员知道一切事物的好处，却不知道任何事物的权衡。”

Where Should You Invest Your Time?

Intuition grows with experience, and over the years you will start to have a sense of what things have staying power and what is probably just a flash in the pan. Ultimately, you’ll see where the trends are taking the industry. You should temper your hunches a bit, though. Paul Graham once wrote of the hacker’s radar, describing some of the criteria he considers when looking at a new technology. After applying that hacker’s radar to Java, he concluded that “I have a hunch that [Java] won’t be a very successful language.” Now, he made this statement in 2001 when Java was fairly new. More than 20 years later, with the full value of hindsight, Java is obviously one of the most successful languages of all time. If someone as experienced and successful as Graham can be that wrong, you may want to temper your own intuition a bit.

直觉随经验增长，多年之后你会开始有感觉：哪些东西有持久力，哪些可能只是昙花一现。最终，你会看到趋势把行业带向何方。不过，你应该稍微收敛一下自己的预感。Paul Graham 曾写过“黑客雷达”，描述他评估一项新技术时考虑的一些标准。把那套黑客雷达用在 Java 上之后，他总结说：“我有预感，[Java]不会是一门很成功的语言。”注意，他说这话是在 2001 年，当时 Java 还相当新。20 多年后，事后看来，Java 显然是有史以来最成功的语言之一。如果连 Graham 这样经验丰富、如此成功的人都能错得这么离谱，你可能也要稍微收敛一下自己的直觉。

That said, judging covers can be useful. In software, patterns often repeat themselves, and things tend to swing like a pendulum between extremes. It is common for old things to be dusted off, refined, renamed, and introduced again as if no one has ever done that before. Consider this description:

话虽如此，“看封面”也可能有用。在软件里，模式经常重复，事情像钟摆一样在两个极端之间摆动。旧东西被掸灰、精炼、改名、再拿出来，好像以前没人做过一样，这种事很常见。看看这段描述：

“An approach that allows software components written in different programming languages and running on various computers to communicate and work together.”

“一种允许用不同编程语言编写、运行在不同计算机上的软件组件相互通信、协同工作的方法。”

What technology do you think that definition describes? Are you thinking about microservices? It fits! However, that’s a definition of Common Object Request Broker Architecture (COBRA), which was popular in the mid to late 1990s, many years before anyone had even contemplated a microservice architecture.

你觉得这个定义描述的是哪项技术？你想到微服务了吗？它确实符合！然而，这是公共对象请求代理体系结构（Common Object Request Broker Architecture，COBRA）的定义，它在 1990 年代中后期很流行，比任何人开始考虑微服务架构早了很多年。

With experience, you will start to see how a new technology is just like one you used a few years back.10 Maybe problems with that technology have been resolved, or maybe not. You should ask probing questions. Just because something is new doesn’t mean it will benefit your projects.

随着经验积累，你会开始看到一项新技术其实就像你几年前用过的某个东西。10 也许那个技术的问题已经解决了，也许没有。你应该问一些探询性的问题。新，并不意味着它会让你的项目受益。

The wisdom of the crowd can be a helpful guide. What is capturing the attention of the community? That can lead you to interesting things. But sometimes the masses get caught up in the hype. Again, apply your own experiences as well.

群体的智慧可以是有用的指引。什么在吸引社区的注意力？那可以带你发现有趣的东西。但有时候大众会被炒作裹挟。再强调一次，也要运用你自己的经验。

10 Or a technology initially created for one purpose may later re-emerge to solve a different problem. For example, the internet was repurposed for civilian use after being initially developed by the military.
或者，一项最初为某个目的创造的技术，后来可能重新冒出来解决另一个问题。例如，互联网最初由军方开发，后来被转作民用。

You can avail yourself of industry resources such as the Technology Radar from Thoughtworks. Updated twice a year, the Technology Radar is a snapshot of tools, techniques, platforms, languages, and frameworks. The radar assimilates experiences across multiple projects to generate as objective an analysis of technology as possible. Tracking the Radar can introduce you to new things as well as providing a sense of where those technologies are in the adoption cycle.

你可以利用行业资源，比如 Thoughtworks 的技术雷达。技术雷达每年更新两次，是工具、技术、平台、语言和框架的快照。雷达吸收多个项目的经验，尽可能客观地分析技术。追踪雷达既能让你发现新事物，也能让你感知这些技术处于采用周期的哪个位置。

Build Your Own Technology Radar
打造你自己的技术雷达

Hopefully, your company offers a rich set of learning opportunities that you can take advantage of. However, as a software engineer, you are ultimately responsible for your career journey. With a never-ending river of new languages and technologies, it can be incredibly challenging to decide how to allocate your precious attention. It is very easy to get stuck in analysis paralysis, something you can short-circuit by building your own technology radar. It doesn’t have to be overly complex nor does it need to be as graphically impressive as the Thoughtworks product. But establishing the habit of periodically checking in with what you find interesting and exciting can make all the difference in your learning. You can read more about how to do so in Chapter 14.
希望你的公司提供了丰富的学习机会供你利用。然而，作为软件工程师，你最终要对自己的职业旅程负责。面对永不枯竭的新语言和技术之河，决定如何分配你宝贵的注意力会非常有挑战性。你很容易陷入分析瘫痪，而打造自己的技术雷达可以短路这种状态。它不必很复杂，也不必像 Thoughtworks 的产品那样在视觉上令人印象深刻。但养成定期审视自己觉得有趣、兴奋的东西的习惯，会让你的学习大为不同。怎么做可以参见第 14 章。

Practice Innovation

As you learn and explore, you will find something that absolutely will benefit your project, your team, or your organization. Bringing those ideas into your organization can give you increased visibility in your company, helping you earn raises and promotions. But how do you go about introducing new things?

当你学习和探索时，会发现某样东西绝对能让你的项目、团队或组织受益。把这些想法带进你的组织，可以提升你在公司的可见度，帮你获得加薪和晋升。但你该如何引入新事物呢？

A book club can be one of the simplest and most effective ways to bring in new technologies. Find a group of like-minded engineers, pick a technical book, and have at it. Try to meet weekly, perhaps first thing in the morning or over lunch. Nearly every organization will cover the cost of books, and many are even willing to pick up catering for lunch or breakfast. Book clubs also serve as motivators: it’s a lot easier to read a chapter when you know you’re talking about it with your team on Tuesday.

读书俱乐部可以是引入新技术最简单、最有效的方式之一。找一群志同道合的工程师，挑一本技术书，开干。尽量每周聚会，也许是早上刚上班时，或午饭时间。几乎每个组织都会承担书费，很多甚至愿意承担午餐或早餐的餐饮。读书俱乐部也是一种激励：当你知道周二要和团队讨论某一章时，读这一章就容易多了。

Many organizations practice some variant of innovation day, often called hacker days or hackathons. No matter the term, the concept is the same: provide people a safe, hands-on space to explore new technologies. Hacker days act like a relief valve for the inevitable desire to play with new technology. Without it, many developers will try to just sneak that new library or language into a project, betting on the utility of asking for forgiveness later rather than asking for permission.

很多组织都会搞某种形式的创新日，常被称为黑客日或黑客马拉松。不管叫什么，概念都一样：给人们一个安全的、动手的空间去探索新技术。黑客日像一个泄压阀，释放那种必然存在的“想玩玩新技术”的欲望。没有它，很多开发者会试图偷偷把新库或新语言塞进项目里，赌的是“事后请求原谅比事前请求许可更容易”。

If your company doesn’t have a recurring hacker day concept, introduce it! Pitch it as an experiment and start small—maybe even just a Friday afternoon. Involve as many

如果你的公司没有定期的黑客日概念，把它引入进来！把它作为一个实验来提案，从小处开始——也许就一个周五下午。让尽可能多的

原书第 305 页

parts of your organization as you can; you’ll be surprised by just where some game-changing ideas lay dormant. While the resulting code may never see production, you will learn something. Maybe a new framework seemed really promising, but when it made contact with your particular context, you quickly realized it would require a near ground-up rewrite. Perhaps that new language elegantly solves a tricky problem you’ve been struggling with for weeks. You won’t know until you try it.

部门参与进来；你会惊讶地发现，一些改变游戏规则的想法正潜伏在什么地方。虽然产出的代码可能永远上不了生产环境，但你会学到东西。也许某个新框架看起来很有前途，但当它接触到你的具体环境时，你很快意识到它几乎要重写整个系统。也许那门新语言优雅地解决了你纠结了几周的棘手问题。不试不知道。

Periodic project showcases, whether department-wide or companywide, are an excellent way to learn what technologies are being used in your organization. The mechanics range from short, lightning-talk-length demos all the way to a set of booths, where different groups present their work. Demo days are not only a great way to learn about the technologies being used in the company, but also an opportunity to identify the people you can go talk to when a need arises on your project.

定期的项目展示会，无论是部门级还是公司级，都是了解组织里正在用什么技术的好办法。形式从短到闪电演讲的 demo，到一排展位、不同小组展示自己的工作，不一而足。Demo 日不仅是了解公司所用技术的好方式，也是一个识别“当你项目上有需求时可以去请教谁”的机会。

Hackathons aren’t the only innovation option. Regular tech talk series are an invaluable way to introduce new concepts into a company. Whether the speakers are sourced from your colleagues or industry experts, providing a steady diet of lunch-and-learn sessions is one of the simplest ways to keep up with the changing technology landscape.11 Again, if your company doesn’t have an existing talk series, create it! Volunteering to deliver a talk on a technology you’re trying to learn is a powerful motivator.

黑客马拉松并不是唯一的创新选择。定期的技术讲座系列是把新概念引入公司的宝贵方式。无论讲者来自你的同事还是行业专家，持续提供午餐学习会是跟上技术格局变化最简单的方式之一。11 再强调一次，如果你的公司没有现成的讲座系列，自己办一个！自愿就你正在学的技术做一次演讲，是强大的动力。

Lunch-and-learn sessions don’t need to be companywide to be effective. More localized approaches are great too. Have you read an interesting article or watched an insightful video? Share it with your team. Looking for some extra motivation to read a new book? Start a book club with a few like-minded souls, trading off who is responsible for leading the discussion. If you’re really excited about new technologies, start a biweekly tech discussion meeting!

午餐学习会不必是公司级才有效。更局部的方式也很好。你读了一篇有趣的文章或看了一段有洞见的视频吗？分享给你的团队。想找点额外动力读一本新书？和几个志同道合的人办个读书俱乐部，轮流负责主持讨论。如果你对新技术真的很兴奋，办一个双周技术讨论会！

Most decent-sized metropolitan areas have a regular schedule of local meetups and user group meetings. Odds are, you can find an interesting tech talk most evenings (and you’re likely to get dinner or at least some refreshments out of the deal).12 While the large industry events in Las Vegas or San Francisco may get more attention from the tech press, there are many excellent regional events that won’t require you to spend thousands of dollars on travel.

大多数像样的大城市都有定期的本地聚会和用户组会议。很可能，你几乎每个晚上都能找到一场有趣的技术讲座（而且你很可能还能蹭到晚餐或至少一些茶点）。12 虽然拉斯维加斯或旧金山的大型行业活动可能获得科技媒体更多关注，但也有很多出色的区域活动，不需要你花几千美元差旅费。

If you’ve already got a well-attended lunch-and-learn series, and you’ve attended a regional event, you could take things up a notch and organize an internal conference. These can range from informal half-day events with a handful of internal speakers to full-on multiday, multisite affairs including industry experts from outside your

如果你已经有一个参与度不错的午餐学习系列，也参加过区域活动，可以再上一个台阶，组织一次内部大会。形式可以从非正式的、半天、几位内部讲者的活动，到包括外部行业专家在内的、多日、多站点的正式活动，

11 Or as one organization termed it, “chew and spews.” Not our preferred moniker, mind you.
或者用某家公司的说法，叫“嚼了吐出来”。请注意，这不是我们偏爱的叫法。
12 Volunteering to give a talk at a local event is an excellent on-ramp to conference speaking if that path is of interest to you.
如果你对大会演讲感兴趣，自愿在本地活动上讲一次是极佳的入门通道。
原书第 306 页

organization.13 Do not underestimate the effort it takes to organize and deliver on even small internal events. But the payoff can be huge.

都可以。13 不要低估组织和交付哪怕是小型内部活动所需的努力。但回报可能是巨大的。

Internal events bring people together and help new ideas spread. They offer a chance for people to interact with those they don’t normally encounter day to day. They are also an excellent chance for you to put your presentation skills to the test. While presenting provokes primal fear in many, it is an excellent motivator if you’re trying to learn something new. Not to mention the visibility can accelerate your career growth, setting you up for a promotion or increased project responsibility.

内部活动把人们聚在一起，帮助新想法传播。它们提供机会让人们和平时日常碰不到的人交流。它们也是你测试演讲技能的绝佳机会。虽然演讲让很多人感到原始的恐惧，但如果你想学新东西，它是极好的动力。更不用说，可见度可以加速你的职业成长，为晋升或承担更多项目责任铺路。

Architectural Briefings

Some organizations have a formalized approach using architectural briefings. Essentially one person does some research and presents the results back to the team. And no, you don’t have to be an architect to deliver an architectural briefing. While there are any number of questions you can explore, you should be sure to hit on these:

有些组织有一种正式的做法，叫架构简报。本质上就是一个人做调研，然后把结果讲回给团队。而且，做架构简报不要求你是架构师。虽然你可以探讨的问题有很多，但一定要覆盖以下几点：

  • Why should you use this technology? Why should you not use this technology?你为什么应该用这项技术？你为什么不应该用这项技术？
  • What do you need to know in order to answer the previous question?要回答上一个问题，你需要知道什么？
  • What do you need to know in order to use this technology?要使用这项技术，你需要知道什么？

The resulting presentation doesn’t need to be a multiple-hour affair; 45–60 minutes is more than sufficient. It isn’t a deep dive how-to but should get beyond the basic Getting Started documentation. These sessions should be interactive and encourage two-way participation. Attendees should be taking notes and asking good questions, bringing their own experiences to bear on the topic.

最终的演讲不需要长达数小时；45–60 分钟绰绰有余。它不是深度动手教程，但应该超越基础的入门文档。这些场次应该是互动的，鼓励双向参与。与会者应该记笔记、问好问题，把自己的经验带到话题里。

If you get past the briefing phase, it’s time to roll up your sleeves and get your hands dirty. It’s time for a workshop. Unfortunately, you will never get enough time to perform a workshop. Trying to decide between two competing frontend technologies? There’s a surefire way to make that choice: build the app twice, once with each, and throw away the one you don’t like. Good luck getting that approved.14 You will have to determine the most important things to prove with your limited time. Focus on exploring the key features and have a simple setup for participants. Clearly state your objectives and offer follow-up material for those who wish to dig deeper after the session. Don’t be afraid to try things out and poke around the nooks and crannies; you may be pleasantly (or unpleasantly) surprised by what you discover. What works? What doesn’t? What happens when you venture off the happy path?

如果过了简报阶段，就该卷起袖子动手了。该办工作坊了。不幸的是，你永远不会有足够的时间来做工作坊。想在两种相互竞争的前端技术之间做选择？有一个包你满意的办法：把应用写两遍，每种技术一遍，把你不喜欢的那个扔掉。祝你能争取到批准。14 你必须决定在有限时间内最需要验证的事情是什么。重点探索关键特性，为参与者准备简单的环境。清楚地陈述你的目标，并为想在会后深入钻研的人提供后续材料。不要害怕动手试、去犄角旮旯里戳一戳；你可能会惊喜（或惊怒）地发现一些东西。什么管用？什么不管用？当你偏离快乐路径时会发生什么？

13 Your authors have participated in many of these events for our clients; reach out if we can help.
你们的作者曾为客户参与过很多这类活动；如果我们能帮忙，尽管联系。
14 If you ever succeed, please drop your authors a note; we’d love to hear more.
如果你真的成功了，请给你们的作者捎个信；我们很想听听。
原书第 307 页

Ensure that your workshop is subject to any constraints the technology will encounter on the target project. If you will be adding this to an existing legacy project, test the technology with those legacy limitations. Getting something to work in a greenfield environment can be helpful but may leave you with an incomplete picture.

确保你的工作坊考虑到这项技术在目标项目上会遇到的任何约束。如果你要把它加到一个已有的遗留项目里，就在那些遗留限制下测试这项技术。在全新环境里跑通某个东西可能有帮助，但也可能让你看到的画面不完整。

Legacy Project Constraints
遗留项目的约束

Nate here. Years ago a participant in one of my workshops shared their experience trying to use a new user interface technology on their project. They had hit a wall with the library they had chosen years before and needed to make a change. The team surveyed the field, narrowing the options to three. They divided up the libraries and performed some greenfield workshops. Eventually they settled on one option that they planned to sprinkle into their application.
Nate 来说两句。多年前，我一个工作坊的参与者分享了他们尝试在项目中使用一种新 UI 技术的经历。他们多年前选的库撞到了墙，需要换。团队调研了一圈，把选项缩到三个。他们分工各做了一些全新环境的工作坊。最终选定一个，计划零星地撒进他们的应用里。
Six months later they now fully realized this library couldn’t be added in here and there; to truly use it, they would need to completely refactor their application. They admitted they’d been caught up in the hype around the library they chose, but it’s also clear they should have performed their exploitation using a fork of their existing project. They likely would have discovered the need for a greater refactoring much earlier. Now, it is possible they would still have chosen that library! But at least they would have gone into it eyes wide open.
六个月后，他们完全意识到这个库不能这里加一点那里加一点；要真正用上它，他们需要彻底重构整个应用。他们承认自己被所选库的炒作裹挟了，但也清楚，他们本应该用现有项目的一个分支来做探索。那样很可能早就发现需要大重构。当然，他们最后可能还是会选那个库！但至少他们会睁大眼睛进去。
The moral of the story: just because you can get the to-do list to work greenfield doesn’t mean a given technology will survive contact with your environment. You play how you practice; don’t try new things in a vacuum.
这个故事的寓意：你能在全新环境里把待办清单跑通，并不意味着某项技术能在和你的环境接触后存活。怎么练就怎么打；不要在真空里试新东西。

Once you’ve had some hands-on time, you can make informed decisions about a technology. If everything checks out, it’s time to find a trial project in your organization. Make sure the trial project is a good fit and ensure that a failure won’t doom a critical strategic project.

一旦有了一些动手时间，你就可以对一项技术做出知情决策。如果一切都核查通过，就该在组织里找一个试点项目。确保试点项目合适，并确保它失败不会毁掉一个关键的战略项目。

Practice Grace

Keeping up with the rapidly changing technology landscape is important and, frankly, a vital part of your software engineering skill set. However, it can be very overwhelming. Be kind to yourself; practice some grace. It can be incredibly easy to burn out by trying to stay on top of an industry as diverse as software. Learning should be fun, not a point of stress in your life. Don’t let it come at the expense of a good night’s sleep or your mental (or physical) health.

跟上快速变化的技术格局很重要，坦白说，它是你软件工程技能组合中至关重要的一部分。然而，它也可能让你非常应接不暇。对自己好一点；修炼一点从容。想跟上软件这么一个庞杂行业的最前沿，非常容易 burnout。学习应该是有趣的，而不是你生活中的压力源。不要让它以牺牲一夜好眠或你的心理（或身体）健康为代价。

There’s nothing wrong with waiting until the last responsible moment to learn something. Technology is full of hype cycles; don’t be afraid to let something play

等到最后一个负责任时刻再学某样东西，没什么不对。技术充满了炒作周期；不要害怕让某样东西先演完

原书第 308 页

out before you commit your time to it.15 Patience is a virtue; the software space is littered with the abandoned remains of last month’s new hotness. There’s no statute of limitations on when you can learn something: if something proves it has staying power, you can always pick something up next week or next month or next year.

你再投入时间。15 耐心是一种美德；软件领域里到处都是上个月新热点的残骸。你什么时候学某样东西，并没有诉讼时效：如果某样东西证明了自己有持久力，你下周、下个月、明年随时都可以捡起来。

Wrapping Up

Technology changes. Fast. Over the course of your career, you will work with a wide variety of tools, languages, and technologies; your ability to learn, adapt, and adjust is vital to your success. Keeping your skills up-to-date must be a habit, so block out time in your schedule to play with new things. A regular cadence is more sustainable than cramming a year’s worth of learning into a long weekend. Enjoy the process!

技术在变。很快。在你的职业生涯中，你会和各种各样的工具、语言和技术打交道；你学习、适应、调整的能力对你的成功至关重要。让技能保持最新必须成为习惯，所以在日程里留出时间玩新东西。有规律的节奏，比把一年的学习塞进一个长周末更可持续。享受这个过程！

Putting It into Practice

Ultimately, to learn a new technology, you have to literally put it into practice. Consider building a personal app to scratch an itch; maybe you want to manage your burgeoning wine collection or you want to build an application to keep track of your child’s sports statistics. If you don’t have any burning needs, reach out to your local school or nonprofits, as they’re often looking for technology help and will usually give you wide latitude to try things out.

最终，要学一项新技术，你必须真的把它付诸实践。考虑做一个个人应用来挠自己的痒处；也许你想管理自己日益增长的葡萄酒收藏，或者想做一个应用来跟踪孩子的运动数据。如果你没有什么迫切需求，联系一下当地学校或非营利组织，他们常常在找技术帮手，而且通常会给你很大的自由度去试东西。

Take a moment to survey the technology field; what is generating the most interest today? Does it speak to you? If not, pick something that does! Go deep on the thing that excites you, follow the thought leaders on social media, and subscribe to podcasts, streams, newsletters, and videos. Is there a local user group you can attend? Are there any conferences focusing on it? What about virtual events? Immerse yourself in that space. Try building a personal project using it. Give a presentation on it to your colleagues, at your local user group, or at a conference.

花一点时间俯瞰技术领域；今天什么最引人关注？它对你有吸引力吗？如果没有，挑一个有吸引力的！深入钻研让你兴奋的东西，在社交媒体上追随思想领袖，订阅播客、直播、newsletter 和视频。有没有你可以参加的本地用户组？有没有相关的会议？虚拟活动呢？把自己沉浸在那个领域里。试着用它做一个个人项目。就它给你的同事、本地用户组或会议做一次演讲。

Every month or two, reassess. Are you still passionate about that technology? If not, pick something new! Rinse and repeat. Don’t be afraid to return to something you explored earlier; you won’t have to relearn everything, and you’ll likely expand on your knowledge.

每一两个月，重新评估一下。你对那项技术还有热情吗？如果没有，换个新东西！如此反复。不要害怕回到你以前探索过的东西；你不必从头重学一切，而且很可能会在原有知识上扩展。

At the end of the day, nothing is quite as effective as spending a few days or weeks producing working code. It doesn’t have to be elegant, doesn’t have to cover every possible edge case, and can be just enough to prove the technology out. There are no shortcuts to learning, no way to just “load the information into your head.” Learning out loud can also be an effective teacher. Don’t be afraid to join forces with a couple of friends or colleagues working through a small project together.

说到底，没有什么比花几天或几周产出能跑的代码更有效。它不必优雅，不必覆盖每一个可能的边界情况，只要足够验证这项技术就行。学习没有捷径，没法“把信息直接装进脑子”。大声学习也可以是一位好老师。不要害怕和几个朋友或同事联手，一起做一个小项目。

15 Time is a nonrenewable resource. Spend it wisely.
时间是不可再生资源。明智地花它。
原书第 309 页

Even just one additional set of eyes can help, so pairing is an effective approach. Consider open sourcing your project or at least hosting it on a public repository so others can comment and contribute. You could also consider live streaming your learning; while it can be intimidating, the communal effect is powerful. Others have likely encountered similar problems and will typically offer their advice. Just the simple realization that you aren’t alone on your learning journey can be incredibly reassuring.

哪怕只是多一双眼睛也有帮助，所以结对是一种有效方法。考虑把你的项目开源，或者至少托管在一个公开仓库里，让别人可以评论和贡献。你也可以考虑直播你的学习过程；虽然可能让人发怵，但社群效应是强大的。其他人很可能遇到过类似问题，通常会给出建议。仅仅是意识到“学习路上你不是一个人”，就能让人非常安心。
